lesson.grammar_point: future perfect and future continuous for commitments in a closing address

listenings.text: Most speakers treat the ending as the moment to relax, and the audience can feel it. They say that is all, or they thank twenty people by name, and the energy of the room drains away before the applause. I teach executives to plan the last three minutes before they plan anything else. Start with a recap, in one sentence, of the idea that connected everything. Then turn the agreements into commitments: who will have done what, and by when. Then give the room a picture of the future, so that the next meeting already feels real. End with one call to action, not three. And only then say thank you. The last thing the room hears is the first thing it remembers.

If there is one idea to take home from these two days, it is this: the region does not lack capital. It lacks contracts that people trust. So let me turn our agreements into commitments. By the end of March, the ministry will have published its draft concession model. By June, the development bank will have shared a term sheet for a first-loss guarantee. And by the time we meet again in September, at least three funds in this room will have named a project they are studying. We will track all of it on a public scorecard. This time next year, I hope we will be discussing projects under construction, not frameworks on paper. My call to action is simple: follow through on what you said on this stage. And now, with real gratitude, thank you to our sponsors and to all of you.

paras: Every summit ends the same way. The last panel finishes, the host thanks the sponsors, the room applauds, and three hundred people check their flights. Six months later, somebody organizes the next summit and discovers that nothing agreed at the last one was ever done. The problem is not the quality of the debate. It is the last five minutes.

A good closing address does three things, and thanking people is not one of them. First, it names the through line: not a summary of every session, but the one idea that connected them. At a summit on Latin American infrastructure, that idea is rarely money. More often it is trust. Second, it turns agreements into commitments. An agreement that the ministry should publish a draft is a hope. A commitment that the ministry will have published its draft by the end of March, with a name next to it, is an action item.

Third, a good close puts the room in the future. When the host says that this time next year the funds will be discussing projects instead of frameworks, he is not predicting. He is describing a meeting that everyone in the room now has a reason to attend. The best hosts add one more tool: a public scorecard, reviewed at every roundtable, so that following through on a promise becomes visible, and so does failing to.

None of this requires a long speech. The strongest closing addresses last less than three minutes. They recap in one sentence, list three commitments with owners and dates, end with a single call to action, and only then thank the sponsors. By the time the applause starts, the next summit already has an agenda.
